{"passages":[{"reference":"3.41","text":"And Simon said, “You are plainly avoiding hearing from the Scriptures the refutation directed against your God.”

And Peter said, “You yourself seem to me to be doing this. For whoever avoids an orderly course of inquiry does not want a true examination to take place. Therefore, by following the proper order and wishing the author to be identified first, I am plainly one who wishes to travel the straight road.”

And Simon said, “First acknowledge whether what has been written against the creator is indeed true, and whether he is not above all things but, according to the Scriptures, subject to every form of wickedness; afterward we will investigate the one who wrote it.”

And Peter said, “So that I may not seem unwilling to investigate because I oppose your disorderly procedure, I answer: I say that if what has been written against God were true, it would in that case show God to be wicked.”

And Simon said, “How can you establish this?”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"φεύγων ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὸν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ σου ἀκοῦσαι ἔλεγχον","chosen":"avoiding hearing from the Scriptures the refutation directed against your God","rationale":"Takes φεύγων with the infinitive in the sense “avoid doing” and attaches ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν to the source of what is heard. Alternatively, ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν could attach more directly to φεύγων: “fleeing from the Scriptures so as not to hear.”"},{"source_quote":"πρῶτον τὸν συγγραφέα νοηθῆναι","chosen":"the author to be identified first","rationale":"In this dispute about who composed the writings, νοηθῆναι means that the author is to be recognized or ascertained, not merely understood abstractly."},{"source_quote":"τὴν εὐθεῖαν ὁδεύειν","chosen":"to travel the straight road","rationale":"Preserves the source’s road image rather than reducing it to “proceed correctly.”"},{"source_quote":"πάσῃ ὑποκείμενος μοχθηρίᾳ","chosen":"subject to every form of wickedness","rationale":"πάσῃ with the abstract noun is represented idiomatically by “every form of,” while retaining Simon’s sweeping accusation."},{"source_quote":"οὕτω τὸν θεὸν δείκνυσιν μοχθηρόν","chosen":"it would in that case show God to be wicked","rationale":"οὕτω points to the stated condition: if the hostile descriptions were true, they would show God in that way to be wicked."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Πρόδηλος εἰ","issue":"The selected print has εἰ, normally the conjunction “if,” where the syntax strongly supports the second-person copula “you are.” Treating this as an accentual or orthographic error is contextually persuasive but remains a proposed interpretation of the confirmed printed wording.","proposed_reading":"Πρόδηλος εἶ","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"3.42","text":"And Peter said, “Because contrary things have been written against the statements that speak badly of him, neither of the two can be confirmed.”

And Simon said, “How, then, when some scriptural statements call him evil and others good, can what is true be recognized?”

And Peter said, “All the statements of the Scriptures that agree with the creation made by him are true, while all that are contrary prove to be false.”

And Simon said, “How can you show that the Scriptures contradict themselves?”

And Peter said, “You say that Adam came into being blind, which he did not; for he would not have pointed it out to a blind man while commanding him, saying, ‘But from the tree of knowing good and evil, do not taste.’”

And Simon said, “He said that his mind was blind.”

And Peter said, “How could he have been blind even in mind, when, before tasting the plant, he assigned names proper to all the animals in agreement with the one who created him?”

And Simon said, “If Adam had foreknowledge, why did he not foresee the serpent that was going to deceive his wife?”

And Peter said, “If Adam did not have foreknowledge, how did he assign his sons, as soon as they were born, names corresponding to the deeds they would perform? He called the first Cain, which is interpreted ‘jealousy’; and Cain, having become jealous, killed his brother Abel, which is interpreted ‘mourning,’ for their parents mourned over him, the first to be murdered.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ταῖς αὐτὸν κακῶς λεγούσαις φωναῖς τὰ ἐναντία γέγραπται","chosen":"contrary things have been written against the statements that speak badly of him","rationale":"The dative is taken as marking the statements against which contrary claims stand. φωναί here denotes textual statements or utterances, not merely audible voices."},{"source_quote":"οὐδ᾽ ὁπότερον βεβαιωθῆναι δύναται","chosen":"neither of the two can be confirmed","rationale":"ὁπότερον refers to either of the two opposing portrayals, one calling God evil and the other good."},{"source_quote":"τῇ ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γενομένῃ κτίσει","chosen":"the creation made by him","rationale":"Preserves κτίσις as “creation” and the passive description of its having been brought into being by him."},{"source_quote":"οὐ γὰρ ἂν τυφλῷ ἐντελλόμενος ἐδείκνυεν","chosen":"he would not have pointed it out to a blind man while commanding him","rationale":"“Pointed it out” retains the showing or indicating force of ἐδείκνυεν separately from the command expressed by ἐντελλόμενος. The implied object is the tree in the quoted command; the wording does not require a particular physical gesture, and “shown it” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"συμφώνως τῷ κτίσαντι αὐτὸν οἰκεῖα πᾶσιν τοῖς ζῴοις ἐπιθεὶς ὀνόματα","chosen":"assigned names proper to all the animals in agreement with the one who created him","rationale":"οἰκεῖα describes names appropriate or proper to the animals, while συμφώνως expresses agreement or harmony with the creator."},{"source_quote":"Κάιν, ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται ζῆλος","chosen":"Cain, which is interpreted ‘jealousy’","rationale":"ζῆλος can mean “zeal” or “jealousy.” The following ζηλώσας and Cain’s killing of Abel favor “jealousy” here."},{"source_quote":"Ἄβελ, ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται πένθος","chosen":"Abel, which is interpreted ‘mourning’","rationale":"πένθος can denote grief or mourning; the following verb ἐπένθησαν supports “mourning” and preserves the lexical connection."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.43","text":"But if Adam, being God’s work, had foreknowledge, much more did the God who created him. And the statement that is written, “God considered,” is false, as though he had resorted to reasoning because of ignorance. Furthermore, if “the Lord was testing Abraham,” it was so that he might know whether he would endure. And the written statement, “Let us go down and see whether they are bringing matters to completion in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me; but if not, so that I may know”—and, so that I do not greatly prolong the discussion, whatever statements speak of his ignorance or of anything else objectionable are overturned by other statements that say the opposite and are thereby exposed as false.

That he truly foreknows is shown when he says to Abraham, “Knowing, you will know that your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not its own, and they will enslave it, mistreat it, and humble them for four hundred years. But the nation to which they may be enslaved I myself will judge. After these things they will come out here with many possessions. You, however, will depart to your fathers in peace, having been sustained in a good old age. In the fourth generation they will return here, for up to now the sins of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐνεθυμήθη ὁ θεός","chosen":"God considered","rationale":"ἐνθυμέομαι can mean consider, reflect, or take thought. “Considered” retains the alleged act of deliberation that the author connects with reasoning from ignorance."},{"source_quote":"ὡς λογισμῷ χρησαμένου διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν","chosen":"as though he had resorted to reasoning because of ignorance","rationale":"The genitive construction characterizes the quoted statement as implying that God used deliberative reasoning because he lacked knowledge."},{"source_quote":"ἔτι μὴν καὶ εἰ „ἐπείραζεν κύριος τὸν Ἀβραάμ“, ἵνα γνῷ εἰ ὑπομενεῖ","chosen":"Furthermore, if “the Lord was testing Abraham,” it was so that he might know whether he would endure","rationale":"The purpose clause is retained as the consequence of the conditional wording. The sentence may alternatively be understood elliptically as identifying another written statement that the author regards as false."},{"source_quote":"εἰ κατὰ τὴν κραυγὴν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐρχομένην πρὸς· μὲ συντελοῦνται","chosen":"whether they are bringing matters to completion in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me","rationale":"This rendering preserves the completion or carrying-through component of συντελοῦνται while understanding the verb as describing conduct corresponding to the outcry. Alternatives include “whether they are carrying matters through according to their outcry” and, with a more passive sense, “whether they are being brought to completion according to their outcry.”"},{"source_quote":"ὅσαι ποτὲ φωναὶ ἀγνοίας αὐτοῦ καταλέγουσιν ἢ ἄλλο τι χαλεπόν","chosen":"whatever statements speak of his ignorance or of anything else objectionable","rationale":"χαλεπόν can mean difficult, harsh, severe, or objectionable; here it denotes some other adverse claim about God."},{"source_quote":"γινώσκων γνώσῃ","chosen":"Knowing, you will know","rationale":"Preserves the emphatic repetition of the cognate participle and verb rather than replacing it with the familiar but less source-transparent “know for certain.”"},{"source_quote":"δουλώσουσιν αὐτὸ καὶ κακώσουσιν καὶ ταπεινώσουσιν αὐτοὺς","chosen":"they will enslave it, mistreat it, and humble them","rationale":"The translation preserves the source’s shift from singular αὐτό, referring to the offspring collectively, to plural αὐτούς. Smoothing all the pronouns to either singular or plural would conceal the wording."},{"source_quote":"μετὰ ἀποσκευῆς πολλῆς","chosen":"with many possessions","rationale":"ἀποσκευή can denote baggage, equipment, or movable property. “Many possessions” conveys the property carried out without suggesting modern travel luggage."},{"source_quote":"οὔπω γὰρ ἀναπεπλήρωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι τῶν Ἀμορραίων","chosen":"the sins of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure","rationale":"This idiomatic rendering represents the perfect form of ἀναπληρόω, literally indicating that the sins have not yet been filled up."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"πρὸς· μὲ","issue":"The selected print is confirmed as having a raised point between the preposition and pronoun, together with the printed accentuation μὲ. Reading the words continuously as “to me” is strongly supported by the syntax, but treating the punctuation and accentuation as editorial oddities remains a provisional interpretation rather than a change to the supplied Greek.","proposed_reading":"πρὸς με","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"3.44","text":"What then? Does not Moses also indicate beforehand the people’s sins and reveal in advance their dispersion among the nations? If he himself gave Moses the ability to foreknow, how did he himself not have it? But he does have it. And if he has it, as we have shown, then the written phrases “he considered,” “he regretted,” and “I will go down and see,” and all such expressions are superfluous. These things, having been foreknown before they occurred just as they were going to turn out, receive, through wise administration, an outcome not to be regretted.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὴν διασπορὰν τὴν εἰς τὰ ἔθνη","chosen":"their dispersion among the nations","rationale":"εἰς literally presents movement into the nations; “among” expresses the resulting distribution without losing its destination."},{"source_quote":"περισσόν ἐστιν","chosen":"are superfluous","rationale":"περισσός here means unnecessary, redundant, or superfluous in light of divine foreknowledge. The plural English verb accommodates the listed expressions, though the Greek uses a singular predicate."},{"source_quote":"μετεμελήθη","chosen":"he regretted","rationale":"μεταμέλομαι denotes regret or a change of mind. “Regretted” fits the contrast with the later ἀμεταμέλητον and does not impose the separate reorientation terminology."},{"source_quote":"ἅτινα πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι ὡς ἀποβαίνειν ἤμελλεν προγνωσθέντα","chosen":"These things, having been foreknown before they occurred just as they were going to turn out","rationale":"ἅτινα is taken as referring to the events represented by the preceding expressions. It could attach more loosely to “all such things,” but their occurrence and outcome favor an event reference."},{"source_quote":"οἰκονομίᾳ σοφῇ ἀμεταμέλητον λαμβάνει τὴν ἔκβασιν","chosen":"receive, through wise administration, an outcome not to be regretted","rationale":"οἰκονομία denotes ordering, management, or administration. “Not to be regretted” preserves the verbal relationship with the preceding “he regretted”; “irrevocable outcome” is another possible contextual rendering."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.45","text":"That he did not desire sacrifices is apparent from the fact that those who craved meat were killed as soon as they tasted it and, after being buried, were called at their grave a “Hill of Desires.” The one who from the outset was angry at sacrificing animals and did not want them sacrificed did not command sacrifices as though he desired them, nor did he demand firstfruits; for without sacrificing animals, neither are sacrifices performed nor can firstfruits be given.

How, moreover, could darkness and gloom and tempest—for this too is written—coexist with the one who formed a pure heaven, created the sun to shine light for everyone, and fixed for the innumerable stars the unalterable order of their courses? Thus, Simon, God’s handwriting—I mean heaven—shows the intention of its maker to be pure and firm.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ δὲ θυσιῶν αὐτὸν μὴ ὀρεχθῆναι","chosen":"That he did not desire sacrifices","rationale":"The articular infinitive makes God’s not desiring sacrifices the claim demonstrated by what follows."},{"source_quote":"ἅμα τῷ γεύσασθαι ἀναιρεθῆναι","chosen":"were killed as soon as they tasted it","rationale":"ἅμα with the articular infinitive indicates that their killing coincided with their tasting; “as soon as” gives this temporal force in natural English."},{"source_quote":"χωσθέντας ἐπὶ τῷ τάφῳ „βουνὸν ἐπιθυμιῶν“ προσαγορευθῆναι","chosen":"after being buried, were called at their grave a “Hill of Desires”","rationale":"The masculine plural participle refers to the people, while the singular predicate names them collectively as a burial mound. Alternatively, the phrase may be understood as compressed wording in which their burial place was called the “Hill of Desires.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ θύσει ζῴων χαλεπαίνων","chosen":"was angry at sacrificing animals","rationale":"χαλεπαίνω denotes anger or indignation, and θύσις here is the sacrificial slaughter of animals."},{"source_quote":"ἀπαρχὰς","chosen":"firstfruits","rationale":"The conventional term preserves the cultic category. In this argument it may include offerings dependent on animal sacrifice, rather than referring only to produce."},{"source_quote":"σκότος καὶ γνόφος καὶ θύελλα","chosen":"darkness and gloom and tempest","rationale":"The three distinct images are retained in order: darkness, thick gloom, and a violent storm or tempest."},{"source_quote":"ἀμεταμέλητον ὁρίσαντι τῶν δρόμων τὴν τάξιν","chosen":"fixed ... the unalterable order of their courses","rationale":"In relation to the stars’ courses, ἀμεταμέλητον denotes an order not withdrawn or revised; “unalterable” conveys that contextual force."},{"source_quote":"τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ χειρόγραφον (λέγω δὲ τὸν οὐρανόν)","chosen":"God’s handwriting—I mean heaven","rationale":"Preserves the image of heaven as something written by God’s own hand rather than reducing χειρόγραφον to a generic “work.”"},{"source_quote":"καθαρὰν καὶ βεβαίαν τὴν τοῦ πεποιηκότος δείκνυσιν γνώμην","chosen":"shows the intention of its maker to be pure and firm","rationale":"γνώμη may mean mind, judgment, disposition, or intention. “Intention” fits the argument that the ordered heaven reveals the maker’s settled purpose; “disposition” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἀπαρχαὶ, δοθῆναι","issue":"The selected print is confirmed as having a comma between ἀπαρχαί and δοθῆναι. The translation provisionally treats it as nonsemantic editorial punctuation interrupting a subject-infinitive construction; no surviving word is omitted or replaced.","proposed_reading":"ἀπαρχαὶ δοθῆναι","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
